prize_parts.citation: For establishing nominal rigidities as the foundation of modern monetary-policy analysis: staggered price and contract setting, policy rules, and a microfounded framework for monetary policy.

statement.case_for: Nominal rigidities and the New Keynesian framework are among the few macroeconomic discoveries that changed both academic modelling and day-to-day institutional practice. Calvo supplies the tractable staggered-pricing mechanism. Taylor supplies staggered contracts and the interest-rate rule. Woodford integrates them into a microfounded framework for optimal monetary policy. These three are the most separable conceptual originators, and each contribution can be named without relying on the empirical DSGE extensions. The work spans about four decades and has been tested through the financial crisis and the 2021-23 inflation. The framework survived with modifications and is still the common language of central-bank analysis. The Committee has not recognised this strand directly, so the prize would not repeat an earlier award. Under common criteria (conceptual depth, breadth of influence, maturity), I judge it the strongest on the shortlist. I accept that its attribution is the least clean.
statement.case_against: The credit is diffuse. Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets and Gertler made major theoretical, empirical and quantitative contributions, and any three-person cut excludes some of them. My own area of research is price-setting, and it supplies a specific scientific reservation. Calvo's time-dependent adjustment is a convenient assumption. Micro evidence from firm surveys and retail price data, including asymmetric adjustment, points to state-dependent behaviour closer to menu-cost models. The framework's performance after 2008 and 2021 also leaves room for a reasonable view that the case is less settled than for B026, where attribution is clean and the empirical record is confirmed.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B007 first and notes that credit within B012 is widely spread, so a three-person selection that omits Calvo or the Christiano-Eichenbaum-Evans group is a significant weakness.
responses.response: I accept the attribution weakness and have not seen an argument that removes it. I still place Calvo, Taylor and Woodford ahead of the estimation-oriented contributors because each originated a distinct conceptual element. B007 has the cleaner two-name core in Kiyotaki and Moore. I rank it below B012 because of its closeness to the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises, which Krusell also notes, and because the empirical support for the collateral channel is mixed. I would not call that a decisive difference, and I keep B007 as an alternative.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B026 first, with Melitz as the central contribution, Helpman as the natural co-laureate and Redding's role more derivative.
responses.response: I agree with the restriction to Melitz and Helpman. B026 is my closest alternative, and it is cleaner than B012 on attribution. The limitation is the Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum work, which is not on this ballot. I put B012 first because of its breadth of conceptual and institutional influence, and not because more members rank B026 in their top three. If the Committee's main concern is attribution cleanliness, B026 is a defensible first choice.

responses.point: Andersson proposes Taylor, Woodford and Gali, treating Gali's canonical New Keynesian model and its empirical evaluation as part of a defensible core.
responses.response: Gali's claim is serious and I regard the choice between him and Calvo as close. I keep Calvo because the New Keynesian Phillips curve rests on his staggered-pricing mechanism, so he is the originator while Gali is the developer and evaluator of what follows. The cost is that Calvo's time-dependence assumption is the part of the framework that the micro price data challenge most. I would not object to a Gali substitution if colleagues find the empirical case more persuasive than the priority argument.

responses.point: Hassler chooses the same trio but notes that the Taylor rule is closer to a rule of thumb than to a deep theoretical result, so Taylor might be weighed less than Calvo and Woodford.
responses.response: I agree the rule alone would be a thinner basis. Taylor's claim also rests on the staggered-contracts model, which is a genuine theoretical contribution and an early version of the nominal-rigidity mechanism. The rule is the part that changed policy practice. Together these justify Taylor's place. The rule by itself would not.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee would prefer Gali, or Christiano and Eichenbaum, in place of Calvo or Taylor.
How much weight to give the post-2008 and post-2021 performance critiques, and the shift toward heterogeneous-agent models, against the framework's institutional influence.
Whether B026 should rank above B012 if attribution cleanliness is given more weight than breadth of policy influence.
Whether the micro evidence on state-dependent price adjustment weakens the Calvo contribution enough to change the proposed names. I have not independently verified this against the literature.
statement.conflict_note: The profile shows two research-field connections. My research on price-setting and menu costs (including a 2026 IJIO paper co-authored with Hassler and Ellingsen) is close to the nominal-rigidities literature in B012, although it is not a work of any credited candidate. My IO background is also close to B024. I co-authored with committee chair John Hassler and former chair Tore Ellingsen on a paper that is not part of any candidate's work. My spouse is a former prime minister, a public fact. No evidence in the profile shows that it bears on any candidate. I disclose these connections without adjudicating them.
